## 5. Earnings Setup Summary

### Revenue Setup

Emaar's reported revenue acceleration — +40% in FY2025 and +23% year-on-year in Q1 2026 — is real but mechanically driven by the conversion of 2021–2024 vintage off-plan sales into IFRS 15 percentage-of-completion revenue, not by new organic demand growth. The AED 134.3 Bn UAE backlog provides genuine near-term revenue insulation: even a 30% drop in new sales in FY2026 would not compress recognised revenue until FY2028–2029 at the earliest. The trajectory is therefore sustainable for at least two to three more years at the level of revenue recognised, but the underlying demand flow that replenishes the backlog is already weakening — unit volumes sold fell 27% in FY2025, and value growth is purely ASP-driven, a pattern that historically precedes volume plateaus. The single factor that would flip revenue direction in the near term is a sustained construction slowdown in Q4 2026 that delays IFRS 15 milestone certification, since Q4 alone carries 32–33% of annual revenue. Reported revenue and underlying forward-looking backlog accretion tell different stories: revenue is printing strongly because old sales are delivering, while the pipeline of new sales feeding future backlog is growing more slowly — an AED ~9 Bn gap in annual accretion rate versus the FY2023–FY2024 pace.

### Margin Setup

The current EBITDA margin corridor of 47%–51% has held for eight consecutive quarters, which is genuine stability — but it reflects a business that has settled post the FY2023 POC anomaly (53.8% EBITDA margin), not one with structural margin expansion ahead. The margin is unlikely to be at a cyclical peak in the absolute sense, but it is at or near the peak that the current product mix (62.7% apartments, 36.5% villas in UAE Development deliveries) and tax regime (13.0% effective rate with DMTT now fully embedded) will allow. The segment or driver that, if it moved adversely by 10–20%, would take the largest consolidated bite is UAE Development gross margin: a 200 bps further compression from apartment-heavy deliveries would reduce consolidated EBITDA by approximately AED 500–700 Mn annually. Emaar's structural margin protection in the malls and hospitality arms (86% and 48% EBITDA margins respectively, backed by contractual lease escalation clauses) acts as a partial floor, but these segments together are only 20% of group revenue and cannot offset a development-segment margin move. Emaar is predominantly a price-taker on construction costs (no pass-through after units are pre-sold), meaning any contractor cost inflation in the Dubai building boom hits the locked-in backlog margins directly with a 2–4 year lag.

### Quality Check

The largest gap between reported and economic earnings is the AED 8,229 Mn of off-plan buyer advance payments that inflate reported FCF (AED 32,524 Mn) above normalised recurring FCF (AED 24,295 Mn) in FY2025 — a 25% overstatement that is structural, not cyclical, and actually widening as the backlog grows. The second largest gap is interest income on ring-fenced project escrow (AED 2,505 Mn, ~14% of reported net income in FY2025), which will mechanically shrink as the escrow is drawn down over the 5–6 year delivery cycle. These two items together mean peak-year EPS embeds declining income streams that are presented alongside genuinely earned operating income without separation. Management's GAAP-to-non-GAAP adjustment (the IFRS 9/15 discount unwinding add-back, worth AED 1,429 Mn) is mechanically sound and recurs every period — it is not genuinely one-time. Modelling normalised earnings for FY2027 would require starting from GAAP earnings, removing the escrow interest contribution as a non-recurring decline, and using the CIQ-reported net income (AED 17,599 Mn attributable to EMAR equity holders) rather than the company's group figure (AED 22,326 Mn, which includes minority interests).

### Consensus Bar

For consensus to be beaten by a material margin in FY2026, the construction delivery pace across 50,800+ UAE units under development would need to hold at or above the FY2025 pace (6,129 units delivered, +44% year-on-year) and Q4 2026 milestone certifications would need to arrive on schedule. Given that the consensus bar was set at AED 53.1 Bn revenue (only ~7% growth over FY2025 actual AED 49.6 Bn) and AED 1.95 EPS, the bar looks undemanding against a backlog that is releasing revenue at a run-rate that already exceeded AED 51.9 Bn on a TTM basis as of Q1 2026. The bar is most likely set too low on revenue (the TTM run-rate already implies ~AED 50–54 Bn before seasonal weighting) and roughly right-to-slightly-low on EPS (which depends on tax timing and escrow interest). The biggest uncertainty is whether the Jun-11-2026 analyst cut was the start of a multi-step revision cycle anchored to structural demand deceleration, in which case the current bar of AED 1.95 could itself be cut further by Q3 2026 results. The consensus embeds no explicit buffer for the Emaar Misr operational deterioration, which is already in filed subsidiary data but not yet fully reflected in group estimates.

## 5b. Leverage & Capital Structure

**Trigger B fires** (material leverage change is not applicable based on the data — the company's strict net debt / EBITDA is near zero at 0.04x FY2025 and -0.72x on the broad basis). However, a **near-term refinancing event of material size is present** that warrants disclosure regardless of the trigger thresholds:

A USD 500 Mn sukuk (Islamic bond) — equivalent to approximately AED 2.75 Bn — matures on September 15, 2026, roughly ten weeks from the date of this analysis. [Capital IQ Capital Structure Details FY2025; 08_earnings-red-flags.md §1, bearish evidence row 4] This maturity falls during the same period as Q2 2026 results (expected around August 12, 2026) and within the delivery window for Q3 2026.

At the most recent period-end (Q1 2026, March 31, 2026): Total Debt = AED 10,064 Mn; Cash & Equivalents (strict, unrestricted per Capital IQ) = AED 12,180 Mn; Short-Term Investments = AED 22,503 Mn. Strict net cash (unrestricted cash minus total debt) = AED 2,115 Mn. Broad net cash (including STI) = AED 24,619 Mn. [Capital IQ Quarterly Financials, Q1-2026 Balance Sheet tab]

The AED 2.75 Bn sukuk is well within the broad net cash position of AED 24.6 Bn, and even within the strict net cash of AED 2.1 Bn when the sukuk is considered against the unrestricted cash balance — the company is not in any distress. However, the company's reported "Net Cash AED 61.7 Bn" (FY2025) includes approximately AED 43 Bn of project escrow cash that is ring-fenced for buyer projects and is not freely available for general corporate use. An investor reading AED 61.7 Bn as freely deployable capital and concluding this sukuk maturity is trivially manageable would be making an error — the actual unrestricted liquidity cushion above the sukuk is AED 2.1 Bn strict or AED 24.6 Bn broad, not AED 61.7 Bn. The company's adjusted EBITDA basis (AED 25,561 Mn) is used in its own credit analysis; on the strict CIQ EBITDA basis (AED 24,132 Mn), the ratio is 0.04x net debt at FY2025. Debt maturity profile beyond the September 2026 sukuk is not fully disclosed in the preliminary results filing; the full FY2025 audited Annual Report (not yet available in English) would contain the maturity schedule. No management commentary or rating-agency action has been noted in the available data pool indicating capital-allocation constraints or the sukuk refinancing is at risk.

## 6. Key Numbers

- **Revenue growth rate (FY2025):** +39.6% YoY to AED 49,557 Mn; TTM Mar-2026: AED 51,858 Mn (+33.4% vs prior TTM) [Capital IQ Annual + Quarterly exports]
- **EBITDA margin (CIQ, FY2025):** 48.7%; Company-adjusted: 51.6%; 8-quarter corridor: 47%–51% [Capital IQ Annual; FY2025 Investor Presentation (Feb-12-2026)]
- **EPS diluted (FY2025):** AED 1.99; Q1-2026: AED 0.57 (+35.7% YoY); TTM: AED 2.13 [Capital IQ Quarterly export]
- **CFO / EBITDA (FY2025):** Reported 139%; Normalised (ex-unearned revenue) ~97%–104% [Capital IQ Annual Cash Flow; 06_earnings-quality.md §2]
- **Biggest driver current level:** AED 134.3 Bn UAE revenue backlog (Dec-31-2025), up 31% YoY; covers 3–4 years of FY2025 delivery pace [FY2025 Investor Presentation, slide 16]
- **Consensus gap (FY2026):** FY2026 EPS consensus AED 1.95 vs TTM EPS AED 2.13 — Street is pricing in a decline on a full-year basis despite a strong TTM run-rate; revenue consensus AED 53.1 Bn vs TTM of AED 51.9 Bn — modest implicit growth [Capital IQ Consensus + Trends exports]
- **Estimate revision direction (last 3 months):** Negative — EPS: 0 up / 3 down; Net Income: 1 up / 4 down; FY2027 EPS cut −14% [Capital IQ Revisions + Trends exports]
- **Earnings volatility score (higher = WORSE):** 38/100 — moderately stable; single variable (POC delivery pace) dominates at AED 2,500 Mn EBITDA sensitivity [07_earnings-sensitivity.md §7]

## 7. What Would Change The Earnings Verdict?

| Current Verdict | What Would Upgrade It | What Would Downgrade It | Data Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mixed earnings setup | Q2–Q3 2026 UAE new property sales confirm volume stabilisation at ≥13,000 units per quarter; Emaar Misr Q1/Q2 2026 EGP-denominated margins recover to >50% (confirming FY2025 collapse was FX-related after all); FY2026 full-year delivery pace holds at 6,000+ units with Q4 milestone cadence intact; English-language FY2025 audited Annual Report confirms no new contingent liabilities or RPT exposure | Q2 or Q3 2026 new UAE property sales data shows unit volumes falling further (below 12,000 units in a quarter); construction delivery delays push Q4 2026 milestones into Q1 2027; Emaar Misr Q2 2026 filing confirms ongoing operational margin deterioration (EGP margins remain sub-40%); a second large analyst EPS cut follows Q2 results; UAE Corporate Tax rate or DMTT scope expanded | Full English-language FY2025 audited Annual Report (IFRS 7 sensitivity tables, RPT note, Emaar Misr segment notes in English); Q2 2026 interim results including new UAE property sales disclosure; Q2 2026 Emaar Misr local-currency financials; earnings transcripts for Q1 and Q2 2026 calls |

## 8. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Dominant earnings trend:** Earnings are executing on a locked-in 2021–2024 vintage backlog — revenue is printing as construction milestones are certified, not because new demand is accelerating. This is an important distinction: the trailing indicator looks exceptional, the leading indicator (unit volumes down 27%, value growth purely ASP-driven) is already softening. Do not conflate the two.

- **Earnings clean and cash-backed:** Partially — GAAP earnings are real and substantiated, but the headline CFO figure (AED 32,524 Mn reported FCF in FY2025) overstates recurring cash generation by approximately AED 8.2 Bn of advance buyer payments that are obligated for project delivery. Interest income on ring-fenced escrow (AED 2,505 Mn, ~14% of net income) will structurally decline as the AED 43 Bn escrow is drawn down. Use normalised FCF (AED 24,295 Mn) and CIQ-attributable net income (AED 17,599 Mn), not company group figures, for valuation.

- **Consensus bar:** The bar looks beatable in the near term: EPS cut to AED 1.95, only 7% revenue growth required, and Emaar has a three-year streak of 11%–23% EPS beats. But the bar's quality depends on whether one analyst's large June 2026 cut is an idiosyncratic overreaction or a prescient structural call — this cannot be resolved from available data. The negative revision breadth (0 up / 3 down on EPS in three months) argues the cut may not be over.

- **Next-quarter setup:** Conditionally favors a Q2 2026 beat — the lowered bar and backlog visibility support this. The bigger risk is Q3 and Q4, which together carry ~58% of annual revenue. The full-year FY2026 beat thesis depends on Q4 milestone timing, which is the single most consequential and most uncertain variable.

- **Top sensitivity variable:** UAE Development backlog POC delivery pace — AED 2,500 Mn EBITDA sensitivity for a ±15% delivery shift. Current direction is positive (units delivered up 44% in FY2025). The delivery and cost inflation risks compound from the same root cause (contractor capacity) and should not be treated as independent bear scenarios.

- **Partial-data cap applied:** Earnings clarity capped at max 70 (no earnings transcripts for FY2025 or Q1 2026 calls). This means management's own characterisation of delivery pace, Egypt, the AED 200 Bn masterplan commitment, and the May 2026 CFO change is unavailable. All management commentary sourced from Level 3–7 documents only.

- **Biggest missing data point:** The English-language FY2025 audited Annual Report is the single highest-value next data request — it would provide IFRS 7 sensitivity tables, the English RPT note, Emaar Misr segment disclosures in a language accessible for full verification, and the full debt maturity schedule including all sukuk and bank facilities beyond the September 2026 maturity.

- **What would change the verdict:** A Q2 or Q3 2026 UAE new-property-sales disclosure showing unit volume stabilisation, combined with an Emaar Misr quarterly EBITDA recovering in EGP terms, would upgrade the verdict from mixed to "Earnings stable" or "Earnings inflecting — positive (backlog-driven)." A second large EPS cut following Q2 2026 results, or confirmed Q4 milestone delays, would downgrade to "Earnings decelerating."

- **Red-flag agent verdict (mandatory propagation):** The `08_earnings-red-flags` agent issued an overall severity verdict of **Critical concerns** — 1 Critical flag, 16 High flags, 6 Medium flags. The single Critical flag is the Emaar Misr EGP-denominated income collapse of 64% with flat EGP revenue, which is already in filed subsidiary data and indicates operational margin deterioration beyond FX. Every High-severity flag from the red-flag agent has been incorporated in Section 1A, Section 3, Section 5b, and the current and downgrade rows of Section 7 above. None have been silently omitted.

- **Conflict between red-flags verdict and beat-miss setup:** The beat-miss agent concluded "Setup favors beat" while the red-flags agent issued "Critical concerns." Both verdicts are correct for their own question: the next-quarter setup is conditionally positive given the lowered bar and backlog mechanics; the structural earnings quality and cycle-position assessment carries Critical concerns. The master synthesizer should treat these as operating on different time horizons rather than treating one as wrong.

## 9. Simple Summary

- Revenue is printing at +40% year-on-year — but this is backlog conversion of 2021–2024 off-plan sales, not new organic demand. The leading indicator (unit volumes sold) is already declining 27%.
- Margins are stable at 47%–51% EBITDA, with no near-term catalyst for expansion; development gross margin declining two years in a row; DMTT permanently shifted the effective tax rate from ~2% to ~13%, which is fully in run-rate.
- Earnings are partially clean — GAAP income is real, but reported FCF overstates recurring cash by ~AED 8 Bn annually and ~14% of net income comes from non-operational escrow interest that will decline as projects complete.
- The consensus bar looks beatable in the near term (EPS cut from AED 2.32 to AED 1.95 in three months, with a strong three-year beat history), but the Jun-11-2026 revision that drove it could be a structural cycle call, not a temporary overcut.
- Next-quarter setup conditionally favors a Q2 2026 beat. The full-year FY2026 thesis hinges on Q3 and Q4, which together carry 58% of annual revenue and depend on milestone timing.
- Biggest sensitivity variable: POC delivery pace — AED 2,500 Mn EBITDA swing for ±15% delivery change. Delivery and cost inflation risks compound from the same contractor-tightness root cause.
- Earnings volatility is moderate (38/100, where higher = worse) — the backlog provides structural insulation, but Q4 concentration creates asymmetric downside if milestones slip.
- This module is useful for the master synthesizer but should be paired with the business-model module's cycle-position and external-dependency assessments to correctly frame the distinction between the strong trailing earnings signal and the softening leading indicators.

# Historical Financials — EMAR (Emaar Properties PJSC, DFM:EMAAR)

**Reporting standard:** IFRS
**Reporting currency:** AED (UAE Dirham), in AED millions unless stated
**Fiscal year end:** 31 December
**Jurisdiction:** United Arab Emirates — Dubai Financial Market (DFM) / DFSA listing rules
**Primary sources:** Capital IQ & Proprietary Data export (FY2021–FY2025 + LTM Mar-31-2026); FY2025 Investor Presentation / Preliminary Annual Report (Feb-12-2026); FY2024 Annual Report (IFRS, audited, Mar-14-2025)

---

## Definitions (§15 compliance)

- **EBITDA** = Operating Income + Depreciation & Amortisation, as computed by Capital IQ from reported IFRS financials. Labelled "CIQ EBITDA" below. The company separately discloses its own EBITDA ("Company EBITDA" / "Adjusted EBITDA") which backs out the finance cost from discounting and unwinding of long-term receivables under IFRS 15 / IFRS 9 — a non-cash item. Section 4 shows both side-by-side.
- **EBIT** = Operating Income as reported by Capital IQ.
- **EPS** = Diluted earnings per share attributable to equity holders of Emaar, in AED. Basic and diluted are identical (no dilutive instruments outstanding).
- **FCF (reported)** = CFO − total capex (absolute value). Capex in the Capital IQ cash flow statement is shown as a negative outflow; absolute value is used per §15 / MODULE_RULES §7.
- **FCF (normalised)** = CFO − capex − Change in Unearned Revenue. Unearned revenue represents net cash advance payments received from off-plan property buyers; these are real cash inflows but represent future delivery obligations. Removing them shows the recurring operating cash the business generates before buyer-deposit inflows. Both FCF figures are shown in Section 1.
- **Net debt (strict basis)** = Total Debt − Cash & Equivalents (unrestricted cash only, per Capital IQ). Positive = net debt; negative = net cash.
- **Net debt (broad basis)** = Total Debt − Cash & Equivalents − Short-Term Investments (financial assets held for liquidity but classified separately from cash by Capital IQ in FY2024 and FY2025). Negative = net cash.
- **Net Cash (company gross-liquidity basis)** = Cash & Cash Equivalents (including ~AED 43 Bn of project escrow accounts) + Short-Term Deposits − Debt. This is the company's own reported "Net Cash" figure (AED 61,655 Mn at FY2025). It is not comparable to either strict or broad net debt above, as it includes project escrow cash that is held on behalf of buyers and is not available for general corporate use. The three bases must not be mixed.

**Revenue CAGR FY2016–FY2025 (company, investor deck):** 14.1%. **Company EBITDA CAGR FY2016–FY2025:** 18.5%. [2]

**Tax rate inflection:** UAE Corporate Tax (9%) was introduced in FY2024; the Domestic Minimum Top-Up Tax (DMTT, 15%) was introduced in FY2025. Effective tax rate moved from 1.5% (FY2023) → 7.7% (FY2024) → 13.0% (FY2025). This is a permanent structural change that permanently reduces after-tax profit growth relative to EBIT growth. [1]

## 4. Reported vs Adjusted Metrics

Two EBITDA figures appear in the data pool for the same periods. These must not be mixed. [1][2]

| Metric | CIQ / Reported Value | Company-Adjusted Value | Adjustment Amount | Adjustment Reason | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| EBITDA FY2025 | 24,132 | 25,561 | +1,429 | Company backs out non-cash finance cost from discounting/unwinding of long-term IFRS 15/IFRS 9 receivables | [1][2] |
| EBITDA Margin FY2025 | 48.7% | 51.6% | +288 bps | Same adjustment | [1][2] |
| EBITDA FY2024 | 17,563 | 19,277 | +1,714 | Same adjustment | [1][2] |
| EBITDA Margin FY2024 | 49.5% | 54.3% | +483 bps | Same adjustment | [1][2] |
| EBIT FY2025 | 22,552 | Not separately disclosed by company | — | — | [1] |
| EPS FY2025 diluted (AED) | 1.991 (CIQ) | 1.99 (investor deck) | Nil | Consistent | [1][2] |

**Note on company EBITDA:** Under IFRS 9, long-term receivables from off-plan property buyers are discounted to present value at inception, and the unwinding of this discount creates a non-cash finance income line each year. Capital IQ includes this in its EBITDA derivation (by adding back all D&A from operating income); the company backs it out to show "operating" EBITDA. Both figures are legitimate. The CIQ figure (AED 24,132 Mn, FY2025) is used throughout this report for consistency and cross-company comparability; the company-disclosed figure (AED 25,561 Mn) is the figure the company's own publications lead with and is the relevant figure for covenant and credit analysis. Downstream agents should distinguish which figure they are using. [1][2]

**Net Cash (company gross-liquidity basis):** The company reports "Net Cash" of AED 61,655 Mn for FY2025 (= AED 52,633 Mn Cash & Cash Equivalents + AED 18,828 Mn Short-Term Deposits − AED 9,806 Mn Debt). The AED 52,633 Mn Cash & Cash Equivalents figure includes approximately AED 43 Bn held in project escrow accounts — cash collected from buyers and ring-fenced for project delivery; it is not freely available for general corporate use. The strict net cash position (unrestricted cash per CIQ minus total debt) was AED −861 Mn (marginally net debt) at FY2025 year-end. The broad net cash position (CIQ unrestricted cash + CIQ short-term investments minus total debt) was AED +17,287 Mn (net cash) at FY2025 year-end. All three figures are legitimate but measure different things; the company's AED 61,655 Mn figure should be read as total project liquidity, not free corporate cash. [2][4]

## 5. Quarterly Seasonality Table (FY2023–FY2025)

Revenue share within each fiscal year and EBITDA margin by quarter, computed from Capital IQ quarterly data. Quarterly sums verified to match annual totals exactly. [3]

| Quarter | FY2023 Rev Share | FY2024 Rev Share | FY2025 Rev Share | Avg Rev Share | FY2023 EBITDA Margin | FY2024 EBITDA Margin | FY2025 EBITDA Margin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 | 23.5% | 18.9% | 20.4% | 20.9% | 45.7% | 51.6% | 50.8% |
| Q2 | 22.3% | 21.6% | 19.6% | 21.2% | 45.4% | 47.6% | 49.2% |
| Q3 | 22.8% | 26.4% | 26.8% | 25.3% | 67.9% | 48.5% | 46.6% |
| Q4 | **31.3%** | **33.0%** | **33.2%** | **32.5%** | 55.8% | 50.3% | 48.8% |

**Seasonality flags:**

1. **Q4 consistently takes >30% of annual revenue** (32.5% average over three years, ranging from 31.3% to 33.2%). Q4 is the single most important quarter. Any disruption to Q4 construction milestones or POC recognition hits annual results disproportionately. Q4-2025 alone contributed AED 16,450 Mn or 33.2% of FY2025 revenue. [3]

2. **Q1 is the weakest quarter** (20.9% average). This creates a structural pattern where the first quarterly print of each calendar year looks seasonally weak on a QoQ basis. Q1-2026 at AED 12,398 Mn was a record Q1 but still fell −24.6% sequentially from Q4-2025. The correct comparison is year-on-year, not sequential.

3. **Q3-2023 EBITDA margin of 67.9% is a clear outlier.** COGS in Q3-2023 collapsed to AED 1,477 Mn against revenue of AED 6,102 Mn (75.8% gross margin for the quarter), driven by a POC project-mix effect in that single period. This inflated the FY2023 full-year EBITDA margin to 53.8%. Since Q1-2024, EBITDA margins have settled into a 47%–51% band, which is the current normalised range.

4. **IFRS 15 POC recognition amplifies seasonal swings** beyond underlying demand patterns. Revenue timing depends on when construction milestones are certified, not on when sales occur. The AED 154.8 Bn total revenue backlog (as of Dec-31-2025) — comprising AED 134.3 Bn UAE backlog and AED 20.5 Bn international — provides approximately 3–4 years of forward revenue visibility at the FY2025 pace, but the quarter-by-quarter release depends on delivery schedules. [2]

## 6. Key Trend Summary

**Revenue direction: Accelerating.** After a −10.6% dip in FY2022 (pandemic-era project delivery cycles normalising), revenue inflected sharply: +7.3% in FY2023, +32.7% in FY2024, +39.6% in FY2025. The LTM Mar-2026 figure of AED 51,858 Mn implies continued growth at scale. Q1-2026 was +22.8% year-on-year. This acceleration is driven by an unprecedented off-plan property sales wave in Dubai that began in 2021–2022 and is now converting to IFRS 15 POC revenue as projects reach construction milestones. The AED 154.8 Bn total revenue backlog locks in at least three to four years of elevated revenue at the current pace, assuming no material delivery delays.

**Margin direction: Inflecting (peak passed, now stabilising).** CIQ EBITDA margins peaked at 53.8% in FY2023 (boosted by a single-quarter POC anomaly in Q3-2023). They compressed to 49.5% in FY2024 and 48.7% in FY2025 and have since held in a 47%–51% range across eight consecutive quarters — this is stabilisation, not ongoing compression. The current margin level is structurally much higher than FY2021's 28.0%, reflecting the shift to higher-margin UAE masterplan projects. Two new structural headwinds are now embedded: (i) the UAE Corporate Tax (9%) effective FY2024 and DMTT (15%) effective FY2025 are compressing net margins faster than EBIT margins (effective tax rate moved from 1.5% in FY2023 to 13.0% in FY2025); (ii) the gross margin settling at 55% vs the FY2023 peak of 63% means any further COGS inflation would compress EBITDA margins from a lower starting point.

**Seasonality: Pronounced.** Q4 consistently captures 32%–33% of annual revenue, making it the dominant earnings period. Q1 is the weakest (21%). The seasonal pattern is structural, driven by IFRS 15 POC milestone timing for large master-community projects. Forward estimates and beat/miss setup must anchor to Q4, not to full-year run-rate arithmetic.

**Inflection points:**
- **FY2022 dip:** Revenue fell −10.6% as COVID-era project deliveries ran off and new sales had not yet converted to revenue. EBITDA grew +19.6% in the same year because project mix shifted to higher-margin completions — the revenue and earnings directions diverged temporarily.
- **FY2023 Q3 POC spike:** COGS collapsed in Q3-2023, pushing quarterly gross margin to 75.8% and FY2023 EBITDA margin to 53.8%. This is a one-time POC milestone effect. Analysts modelling off FY2023 margins will overestimate future margin levels.
- **FY2024–FY2025 re-acceleration:** Record Dubai property sales in 2022–2024 (AED 65.4 Bn and AED 71.1 Bn respectively in UAE new sales) are converting into recognised revenue. UAE Development revenues grew 55% to AED 36,443 Mn in FY2025 and are the dominant earnings driver.
- **FY2024–FY2025 tax regime step-change:** UAE Corporate Tax introduced FY2024, DMTT introduced FY2025. This permanently widens the gap between EBIT growth and EPS growth. The FY2025 effective tax rate of 13.0% is likely to remain near this level or move slightly higher as international operations grow. This is the single biggest structural change to the earnings bridge since FY2021.

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Segment decomposition applied — 3 IFRS reportable segments from business-model module, with 5-bucket management view also available. Segment-level P&L (NPBT) is disclosed for all three segments. Capex by segment is unavailable for FY2022–FY2025 (gap noted in business-model module). The dominant segment is Real Estate / UAE Development at 73–80% of revenue and 66% of group EBITDA — this is the primary analytical focus.

## 2. Revenue Driver Tree

Emaar is a multi-segment real estate developer. The correct revenue formula differs by segment:

| Segment | Revenue Formula |
|---|---|
| UAE Development (73% of revenue) | Units under construction × Percentage of Completion (POC) milestone rate × contract value per unit |
| Emaar Malls (12%) | GLA × occupancy rate × rent per sq. ft. (base rent + turnover rent) |
| International Development (5%) | Units under construction × POC × contract value (EGP/INR/TRY-denominated, then translated at period-average AED rate) |
| Emaar Hospitality (5%) | Hotel keys × occupancy rate × ADR (average daily rate = RevPAR / occupancy) |
| Entertainment, Leasing & Others (5%) | Footfall-linked / fixed contract |

**Consolidated revenue formula:**
> Group Revenue = [UAE Dev units in backlog × weighted POC pace × avg. unit value] + [Malls GLA × occupancy × rent psf] + [Intl Dev POC release] + [Hotel keys × occupancy × ADR] + [Other recurring]

The dominant driver — UAE Development POC release — is a function of (a) the volume of units already sold and sitting in backlog, (b) construction completion pace, and (c) the average selling price locked in at the time of sale. Once units are sold off-plan, the revenue quantum is largely fixed; timing of recognition is what varies.

## 7. Cycle Position (Cycle-Position Rule — Hard Rule)

**Emaar's UAE Development business is at or near the peak of the Dubai residential property cycle as measured by sales volumes and revenue growth rates.** Evidence:

- UAE property sales hit a record AED 71.1 Bn in FY2025, the highest in Emaar's history. Sales value growth was +9% in FY2025 vs +75% in FY2024 and +77% in FY2023 — the growth rate is decelerating at the top.
- Unit volumes sold actually fell: 13,905 units in FY2025 vs 19,058 in FY2024 (−27%). Value growth was ASP-driven, not volume-driven — a late-cycle characteristic.
- The prior cycle trough was FY2020 (revenue −34% vs FY2019), COVID-driven. The prior peak pre-COVID was FY2019 (AED 23.7 Bn revenue). The current cycle has blown far past that peak: FY2025 revenue of AED 49.6 Bn is 2.1× the prior peak.
- The current cycle was driven by (a) the post-COVID global safe-haven / lifestyle shift into Dubai, (b) Russian and Eastern European buyer inflows post-2022 sanctions, (c) UAE Golden Visa and 100% foreign ownership reforms, and (d) government-directed mega-project launches (Al Maktoum Airport expansion, Dubai Square, Creek Harbour). These are not all run-rate drivers: the Russian buyer inflow specifically is a policy/geopolitical tailwind that could reverse. Management has not labelled this cohort separately, so its proportion is not quantifiable from available filings.
- **Revenue backlog mechanics insulate near-term revenue from a demand slowdown:** Even if new sales fell 30% in FY2026–FY2027, the AED 134.3 Bn UAE backlog (at Dec-31-2025) would continue to release revenue for 3–4 years at near-current pace. This is the structural difference between Emaar and a spot-market developer. A sales slump would compress revenue from FY2028–FY2029 onward, not immediately.
- **The current volumes and margins are NOT a normalised run-rate for long-term modelling.** The FY2025 UAE Development revenue growth of +55% is exceptional and reflects the simultaneous maturation of a large 2022–2024 vintage of off-plan sales. A more normalised run-rate — assuming flat new sales from current levels — would imply UAE Dev revenue plateauing around AED 35–40 Bn, not continuing at 40%+ growth.
- **This module agrees with the business-model 10_external-dependency assessment:** the Dubai property cycle is rated "High" external dependence; the cycle is assessed as late-stage expansion, not mid-cycle. One-time policy tailwinds (Russian buyer flows, Golden Visa demand pull-forward, COVID safe-haven premium) should be labelled non-run-rate.

---

## 8. The Single Biggest Revenue Driver

**The pace of construction delivery against the AED 154.8 Bn global revenue backlog (AED 134.3 Bn UAE) is the single biggest revenue driver for Emaar.**

If the quarterly construction completion rate accelerated or slowed by 10–20% relative to plan — due to delivery delays, contractor capacity constraints, or management launch sequencing — the result would be a 10–20% shift in recognised revenue from IFRS 15 POC milestones, moving total group revenue by approximately AED 5–10 Bn in a given year. No other single variable comes close: the backlog is locked-in sales that cannot be un-sold, and its release pace is entirely a function of construction delivery.

The current direction is positive: backlog grew from AED 102.7 Bn (Dec-31-2024) to AED 134.3 Bn (Dec-31-2025) — a 31% increase — meaning the pipeline of future recognised revenue is expanding faster than current deliveries are drawing it down. If sustained, this implies continued double-digit revenue growth for at least FY2026 and FY2027, absent a catastrophic delivery failure.

The bear case is not a demand crash (new sales can fall sharply without affecting near-term revenue, given the backlog buffer), but rather a sustained construction slowdown — contractor labour shortages, materials cost escalation leading to payment disputes, or a regulatory planning freeze — that delays milestone certification. The secondary bear case is a collapse in new sales that depletes backlog accretion from FY2028 onward, with no immediate revenue effect but a visible gap forming in the long-term growth trajectory.

**Reporting standard:** IFRS | **Currency:** AED millions | **Fiscal year end:** 31 December

**Sources:** FY2025 Investor Presentation (Preliminary Annual Report, Feb-12-2026); Q1-2026 Preliminary Interim Report (Apr-08-2026); Capital IQ Annual & Quarterly Financial Exports (FY2021–Q1-2026); FY2024 Annual Report (IFRS, audited, Mar-14-2025)

## Sector Overlay (Step 3b)

**Sector overlay applied: REIT / real estate — margin analysis uses property NOI margin (development gross margin, segment EBITDA margins, and NOI-equivalent metrics) rather than a generic COGS / freight / labour table.**

Emaar is classified in `02_business-identity.md` §3a as a "UAE-dominant luxury residential and master-community developer with a high-margin captive mall and hotel portfolio." The closest SECTOR_OVERLAYS row is **REIT / real estate**, with the note that Emaar is a developer-first business, not a pure REIT. Accordingly:

- The primary margin metric for the **development segment** is gross margin on recognised revenue (the spread between selling price per project and construction/land cost at IFRS 15 percentage-of-completion, or POC — the method by which costs and revenues are recognised in stages as construction progresses).
- The primary metric for the **malls segment** is NOI margin / EBITDA margin on rental income (the net operating profit a landlord keeps after property costs but before depreciation and financing; EBITDA is the closest reported proxy).
- Depreciation is **partially** non-economic for Emaar's investment properties (mall and hotel assets), consistent with the REIT overlay instruction to back it out for operating margin purposes. D&A is reported separately in the IFRS income statement and is shown in Section 3 but not treated as a cash cost for the recurring-business analysis.
- SG&A and corporate costs are disclosed in aggregate as "selling, general and administrative expenses."
- No AFFO / FFO is disclosed, which is a data gap flagged in `02_business-identity.md`.

## 1. Segment Decomposition Status

Segment P&L is disclosed and complete. Three IFRS reportable segments plus an unallocated corporate line are available for FY2025 and prior years. A five-bucket management view (UAE Development, International Development, Emaar Malls, Emaar Hospitality, Entertainment/Leasing/Others) is also disclosed in the investor deck and carries segment-level EBITDA margins. Both views are used below; the IFRS segment figures are authoritative.

**Dominant segment: Real Estate (UAE Development) — 80% of FY2025 revenue, 77% of segment NPBT.**

The business is a single-dominant-segment company by the >85% test at the individual-segment level: UAE Development alone is 73% of group revenue and 66% of group EBITDA. Within the IFRS "Real Estate" segment (80% of revenue), the UAE portion is ~92% and the international portion (mainly Emaar Misr in Egypt) is ~8%. The analysis below proceeds at both the consolidated level and the segment level, with the development segment receiving priority treatment.

**Pass-through lag note:** For the development segment, pricing is locked in at the point of property sale — before construction begins. There is no mechanism to pass through subsequent cost increases to buyers after the sale contract is signed. The lag between a cost increase and its margin impact is therefore the time between when the project was priced (launch date, often 2–4 years before delivery) and when units deliver and costs are charged to COGS under IFRS 15. In practice, construction cost inflation manifests in delivered project margins with a 2–4 year lag. Projects already under construction for delivery in 2026–2028 have locked-in selling prices; any construction cost overshoot directly compresses the "gross margin achieved" of 46–47% reported on the current backlog. For the malls segment, rent escalation clauses are contractual and annual — Emaar can pass through inflation to tenants within 1–3 years as leases (WALT ~2.9 years) renew.

---

## 4. Margin Walk — Which Margin Level Matters Most?

For Emaar, **EBITDA margin** is the right primary operating metric at the group level, but it must be read segment-by-segment rather than consolidated. Here is why:

The group's P&L mixes two structurally different businesses: (a) a property developer where "gross margin achieved" (project-level development margin) and the EBITDA margin on UAE Development (46% in FY2025) are what matter, and (b) an investment property landlord (malls, entertainment, commercial leasing) where NOI margin and EBITDA margin (86% for malls) are the economically meaningful measures and depreciation is non-cash. At the consolidated level, the blended EBITDA margin (48.7% CIQ, 51.6% company-adjusted) is distorted by the development/recurring mix: as the development segment grows faster (73% of revenue) it pulls the consolidated margin toward the lower-margin development margin (46%), even when the malls and hospitality businesses are performing well.

The net profit margin is the least useful primary metric because it now reflects the tax-regime inflection (UAE Corporate Tax + DMTT) as a permanent structural drag — the gap between EBIT growth and EPS growth has permanently widened. Analysts tracking net profit margin trends against history (pre-FY2024 comparisons) are comparing across different tax regimes and will overstate margin compression.

EBIT margin is near-flat (45.5% FY2025 vs 45.4% FY2024) and is the cleanest cross-tax, cross-IFRS-9-adjustment comparison, but D&A inflation from hotel key additions makes it slightly less useful than EBITDA margin for the investment-property arms.

**Summary: Use segment EBITDA margins as the primary operating performance indicator — UAE Development EBITDA margin (currently 46%), Emaar Malls EBITDA margin (currently 86%), and Emaar Hospitality EBITDA margin (currently 48%). At the consolidated level, use CIQ EBITDA margin (48.7%) as the cross-company comparison baseline and flag that net profit margin comparisons are cross-regime post-FY2024.**

## 7. Margin Bridge — FY2025 vs FY2024 (Consolidated)

Where evidence allows, the following bridge decomposes the gross margin change of −246 bps and the net profit margin change of −413 bps.

| Component | Gross Margin Impact (bps) | EBITDA Margin Impact (bps) | Net Profit Margin Impact (bps) | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| UAE Development mix shift (apartments/villas) and product-mix compression | −200 | −100 (partly offset by operating leverage) | −100 | Slide 16 (UAE Dev gross margin 50% FY2025 vs 52% FY2024); Slide 19 (project margin range) |
| Revenue mix shift: development (46% EBITDA) growing 55% vs malls/hospitality (13–15%) | — | −60 (mechanical dilution from development's faster growth) | −60 | Slide 13 (segment revenue and EBITDA shares) |
| Emaar Malls EBITDA margin improvement (84%→86%) | +40 (at consolidated level, given 12% revenue share) | +25 | +25 | Slide 22 (Malls EBITDA 86% vs 84%) |
| SG&A leverage (revenue grew 40%, SG&A grew slower) | — | +50 (estimated; no full-year breakdown) | +50 | Q1-2026 Interim Report (SG&A % comparison); Inference, not from filings for full-year |
| FX impact (Emaar Misr, group FX line: AED −260 Mn vs +AED 505 Mn) | — | −15 (AED 765 Mn swing on AED 35 Bn revenue base) | −15 | 10_external-dependency.md; FY2025 Investor Presentation, slide 21 |
| DMTT tax regime (new in FY2025; added ~5% to effective tax rate) | — | — | −310 (primary driver of NP margin compression) | FY2025 Investor Presentation, slide 12 (footnote); 01_historical-financials.md §1 (effective rate 7.7%→13.0%) |
| Other / unallocated / residual | −86 | −22 | −3 | Balancing item |
| **Total margin change (FY2024 → FY2025)** | **−246** | **−77 (CIQ)** | **−413** | Reconciles to reported figures |

**What the bridge shows:** The gross margin compression of −246 bps and the EBITDA margin compression of −77 bps are both modest and driven by product/segment mix, not by an underlying cost problem. The −413 bps net profit margin decline is almost entirely the DMTT tax step-change, not operational. At the EBIT line (essentially flat, +6 bps), the business is operationally stable.

---

## 8. The Single Biggest Margin Driver

**Construction cost inflation on the AED 134.3 Bn UAE development backlog is the single driver that, if it moved adversely at scale, would compress margins the most.**

Here is the mechanism: Emaar pre-sells units at launch, locking in the buyer's price. It then spends 5–6 years constructing and delivering those units, with revenue recognised under IFRS 15 percentage-of-completion as milestones are certified. All 50,800+ units under construction in the UAE are being built at costs that will be charged to COGS as each milestone is reached. If Dubai's building boom (the same demand wave that drove AED 71.1 Bn of FY2025 property sales) creates sustained contractor cost inflation — tighter skilled labour, higher steel and concrete prices, longer lead times on facade and MEP systems — the cost side of the COGS equation rises while the revenue side (the locked-in selling price) cannot change. The "gross margin achieved" on the backlog, currently disclosed at 46–47%, would compress toward 40% or below on the most-affected cohorts.

Emaar partially protects itself by fixing construction costs with contractors at or shortly after project launch. But in Dubai's current environment, re-tendering and change-order risk is real: the pipeline of concurrent major projects (Emaar alone is building 50,800+ UAE units plus the Dubai Creek Harbour mega-scheme) strains contractor capacity. No single contractor dependency has been disclosed, and no sensitivity table for a given percentage rise in construction costs is available in the data pool — the IFRS 7 market-risk disclosures are in the full FY2025 Annual Report, which has not been filed at the date of this analysis.

**Current direction: Headwind, but contained.** The gross margin achieved on existing backlog is disclosed as stable at 46–47% as of 31 Dec 2025 — construction cost inflation has not yet materially eroded this figure in the reported data. The risk is forward-looking and tied to the pace of Dubai's building activity over the next 2–4 years as the largest cohort of the AED 134.3 Bn backlog delivers.

The tax regime change (UAE Corporate Tax + DMTT) is already embedded in run-rate and is the biggest **actual** margin compressor in the most recent period (−413 bps on net profit margin FY2024 to FY2025). It is not a future risk — it is a permanent structural reset. Construction cost inflation is the biggest **forward-looking** margin risk.

---

## Cycle-Position Note (MODULE_RULES §8)

Emaar is in the **mid-to-peak phase of the Dubai property development cycle** as of the latest reported period (FY2025 / Q1-2026):

- UAE property sales of AED 71.1 Bn in FY2025 are the highest in the company's history by a wide margin, and AED 71.1 Bn compares to AED 65.4 Bn in FY2024, AED 37.4 Bn in FY2023, and AED 30.7 Bn in FY2022. This is a cycle high, not a trough.
- Revenue backlog of AED 134.3 Bn (UAE) is the highest on record. This provides 5–6 years of forward revenue coverage at the FY2025 pace.
- Customer default rate of 0.5% is a cycle-high (low default) metric: in a downturn (COVID 2020), revenue dropped 34% year-on-year from FY2019.
- The precedent cycle: FY2020 saw revenue fall from AED 27.9 Bn (FY2019) to AED 18.4 Bn (−34%) in a single year. The current AED 49.6 Bn revenue base would, in a comparable shock, compress to AED 32–33 Bn — roughly FY2023 levels.
- **The 5–6 year backlog is the key cycle buffer**: even in a demand downturn, Emaar would continue recognising revenue on units already sold (AED 134.3 Bn backlog) for several years. New sales would slow but recognised revenue would not immediately collapse to zero, unlike a spot-delivery model.
- **The government-directed urbanisation tailwind** (Al Maktoum Airport expansion, Dubai Urban Master Plan 2040, Dubai Square Creek Harbour designation) is real but is policy-conditional, not a guaranteed permanent driver. It is treated as a current tailwind, not a run-rate assumption for future margin modelling.

Reconciliation with `10_external-dependency.md`: that module scored external dependency at 52/100 and identified the Dubai property demand cycle as the single biggest lever. This reads consistently with the cycle-peak characterisation here. No divergence.

## 7. Bar Assessment

**Bar is low.**

Three months ago, the Street was modelling FY 2026 EPS at AED 2.32 and revenue at AED 58.2bn. Today those estimates stand at AED 1.95 and AED 53.1bn — cuts of ~16% and ~9% respectively. The primary driver of this compression was a single large revision on Jun-11-2026 (EPS from AED 2.46 to AED 1.93, target from AED 20.50 to AED 15.00), which appears to have followed the Q1 2026 print and a re-assessment of the FY 2026 delivery cadence. Against this sharply lower bar, Emaar's recent track record is one of consistent beats: +11% to +23% EPS surprises across FY 2023–2025, with Q1 2026 also ahead of pre-quarter estimates. The contracted sales backlog of ~AED 127bn globally provides strong revenue visibility, and FY 2026 consensus revenue of AED 53.1bn compares to FY 2025 actual revenue of AED 49.6bn — only a ~7% growth assumption, which looks undemanding given the backlog size and the Q1 2026 run-rate of AED 12.4bn (which annualises to roughly AED 49–50bn before seasonal H2 weighting). In short, estimates have been cut hard, the company has a history of beating, and the bar is now below where it was when the year began.

| Emaar Misr / International Development FX drag worsens | EGP/AED FX (international development) | If EGP weakens further in Q2 2026 vs AED, Emaar Misr's AED-translated EBITDA takes another hit. Emaar Misr's AED-reported EBITDA collapsed from AED 1,559 Mn (96% margin) in FY2024 to AED 479 Mn (31% margin) in FY2025 — an AED 1.08 Bn swing. A repeat of a large quarterly FX loss on the Egypt operation creates headline noise on net income. This is a low-probability severe outcome, not a base case, but cannot be dismissed given no hedging policy is disclosed. | Low | Emaar Misr FX: EGP/AED depreciation ~10.7% vs AED in FY2025 [03_margin-drivers.md §2, §6]; group FX line AED −260 Mn FY2025 vs +AED 505 Mn FY2024 = AED 765 Mn swing [02_revenue-drivers.md §3]; no hedging disclosed [03_margin-drivers.md §2]; Emaar Misr is ~3% of group EBITDA in FY2025 — contained but noisy [03_margin-drivers.md §6] |
| Net interest income declines on rate cuts / lower cash balances | Net interest income line | Emaar held AED 52.6 Bn of cash at FY2025 year-end (including escrow), earning AED 2,505 Mn in interest income in FY2025. If UAE/GCC rates move lower in Q2 2026 (following potential US Fed rate cuts), the quarterly interest income line compresses. A 50 bps rate cut on AED 10–12 Bn of non-escrow cash reduces quarterly interest income by roughly AED 12–15 Mn — a small but visible effect on the EPS line. | Low | Net interest income AED +2,013 Mn FY2025 [03_margin-drivers.md §2]; Q1-2026 net finance income AED 476 Mn [03_margin-drivers.md §2]; Emaar is a net creditor so rate cuts are a mild headwind to net income [03_margin-drivers.md §2] |

---

## 4. What Magnitude Matters?

| Metric | Consensus / Bar | Material Beat Threshold | Material Miss Threshold | Why |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Revenue (AED Mn) | ~AED 10,500–11,000 (Q2 2026, implied from FY2026 consensus AED 53,089 Mn, with Q1 at 12,398 and H2 seasonal weighting) | +AED 1,000 Mn above implied (>+9%) — consistent with the FY2023–FY2025 beat magnitude range of 7–9% | AED 1,000 Mn below implied (<−9%) — in-line with a delivery delay scenario | Emaar has beaten annual revenue by 7–9% in each of FY2023–FY2025 [04_guidance-consensus.md §6]; the same cadence applied to Q2 implies the bar is at approximately the Q2-2025 actual of AED 9,736 Mn plus ~28% YoY for Q2-2026 |
| EBITDA (AED Mn) | ~AED 5,100–5,700 (Q2 2026, implied from FY2026 consensus AED 26,154 Mn) | +AED 500 Mn above midpoint | −AED 500 Mn below midpoint | EBITDA margin corridor has held 47–51% across 8 consecutive quarters; a 200 bps swing on ~AED 10.5 Bn revenue = ~AED 210 Mn |
| EPS normalized (AED) | AED 0.47 (Q2 2026, Capital IQ Trends [04_guidance-consensus.md §4]) | AED 0.52+ (>+10% surprise — consistent with historical beat pattern) | AED 0.42 or below (<−10% miss) | Historical EPS beats range from +11% to +23% [04_guidance-consensus.md §6]; a miss of even −10% would be the first since FY2022 |
| Full-year guidance / backlog disclosure | No formal guidance issued; backlog is the key forward indicator | Q2 2026 new UAE property sales above ~AED 15 Bn (sustaining Q1-2025's record quarterly pace) | New UAE property sales falling below AED 12 Bn (deceleration below the AED 16.5 Bn Q1-2025 record) — would signal backlog accretion slowing | New sales go into the AED 134.3 Bn backlog, not Q2 revenue, but the magnitude disclosed at the Q2 results determines the FY2027–FY2028 revenue trajectory [02_revenue-drivers.md §4; 04_guidance-consensus.md §2] |

---

## 5. In-Line Print But Bad Guidance Risk

| Risk | Evidence | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| In-line current quarter but Q2 new sales number disappoints | The Jun-11-2026 analyst cut that drove the consensus reduction (EPS from AED 2.46 to AED 1.93, target from AED 20.50 to AED 15.00) appears to reflect a re-assessment of the delivery and sales cadence [04_guidance-consensus.md §5]. If Q2 new sales slow materially — even while Q2 recognised revenue meets estimates — analysts will cut FY2027 estimates and the stock reacts negatively to a technically in-line print. | The revenue backlog model means investors lead with the new-sales number as a 3–4 year leading indicator. A shortfall in new sales is more negative for sentiment than a shortfall in recognised revenue, which is largely determined by the delivery schedule already in motion. |
| Beat current quarter on EPS but gross margin on UAE Development falls below 50% | UAE Development gross margin fell from 52% (FY2024) to 50% (FY2025) [03_margin-drivers.md §3]. A further 100–200 bps decline below 50% in a single quarter — from delivery mix or construction cost overshoot — would signal margin pressure on the backlog. If EPS beats because of the tax line while operating gross margin is compressing, the quality of the beat will be challenged. | Analysts focused on the "gross margin achieved" metric (currently 46–47% on the backlog) as a leading indicator of future revenue quality [03_margin-drivers.md §8]. A spot-delivered gross margin well below 46–47% would imply the backlog figure is already stale. |
| Beat EPS due to net interest income or FX, miss quality | If Q2 EPS is ahead of consensus because interest income was higher than assumed or an FX translation benefit appeared, rather than from operating POC revenue or margin expansion, the headline beat would be dismissed. The Jun-11-2026 analyst who cut sharply appears already focused on operational delivery risk, not financial income. | Net interest income AED +2,013 Mn FY2025 is significant (~8% of FY2025 EBITDA) [03_margin-drivers.md §2]; any positive surprise there that masks an operational shortfall would not change the forward earnings picture. |
| Beat revenue but working capital / unearned revenue dynamics raise quality questions | Reported FCF (CFO minus capex) was AED 32,524 Mn in FY2025, but normalised FCF (removing advance customer payment inflows) was AED 24,295 Mn — a difference of AED 8,229 Mn [01_historical-financials.md §1]. If the beat is driven by an unusually large inflow of new customer deposit payments (unearned revenue) rather than earned revenue recognition, reported FCF will overstate underlying cash generation in the period. | The structural off-plan model means CFO regularly includes advance payments that are obligations, not earnings yet. A beat driven by higher advance inflows rather than higher POC recognition is not a durable beat. |

---

## 6. Seasonality Read

Seasonality works against Q2 2026. Over the three years FY2023–FY2025, Q2 has averaged 21.2% of annual revenue — the second-weakest quarter, close to Q1's 20.9% average, and well below Q3's 25.3% and Q4's 32.5% [01_historical-financials.md §5]. The dominant Q4 pattern (33% of annual revenue) is structural: IFRS 15 POC milestone certifications for large master-community projects cluster at calendar year-end. For the Q2 2026 print, investors should not expect a seasonal uplift; the relevant question is whether Q2 2026 holds its YoY growth rate of +20–30% (as Q1 2026 did at +22.8% vs Q1 2025). Seasonality in itself does not create a miss risk for Q2 specifically — the consensus bar already reflects the seasonal pattern — but it does mean that any construction delay in Q2 cannot be "made up" within the quarter, only deferred to Q3 or Q4.

---

## 7. Historical Pattern

Emaar has beaten EPS estimates in every annual period from FY2023 through Q1 2026, with margins of +11% to +23% in FY2023–FY2025 and approximately +9% in Q1 2026 [04_guidance-consensus.md §6]. The one exception in recent history is FY2022, when revenue missed by −3.9% and EPS missed by −10.8% during a normalisation period following the COVID-era property boom. The pattern strongly suggests that Emaar's management does not actively guide the Street, and analysts have consistently set estimates too conservatively relative to what the delivery pipeline and backlog mechanics actually deliver. The synthesiser should weight this pattern meaningfully — it is three consecutive years of material beats against a backlog-driven model that provides structural visibility. However, the FY2022 miss is a live reminder that the pattern can break when the delivery cycle inflects; the current cycle is at or near peak by the metrics in 02_revenue-drivers.md §7, and the risk of a first miss since FY2022 is real if delivery slips or the June 2026 analyst cut proves to be the start of a broader re-rating.

---

## 8. Setup Verdict

**Setup favors beat.**

The weight of evidence — a sharply lowered consensus bar (EPS cut −16% in three months), three consecutive years of large EPS beats (+11% to +23%), AED 134.3 Bn in UAE revenue backlog providing 3–4 years of forward visibility, and an EBITDA margin corridor that has held 47–51% without degradation for eight consecutive quarters — leans toward outperformance. The single most important factor is the lowered consensus bar: the Jun-11-2026 revision drove EPS consensus from AED 2.46 to AED 1.93 in a single move, meaning the current bar is roughly where Emaar was performing two years ago, while the business has continued to grow. The single biggest risk that could flip this verdict is a construction delivery delay in H2 2026 — if the AED 16.5 Bn quarterly new-sales pace stalls or if large project milestones slip out of FY2026, the Q3/Q4 seasonal heavy-lifting (Q4 alone is 33% of annual revenue) may not materialise, and the FY2026 consensus would need to be cut further.

---

## 9. Second-Quarter Look-Ahead

Q3 2026 (July–September) is historically Emaar's second-strongest quarter at an average 25.3% of annual revenue, well above Q2's 21.2%, and typically sees a material sequential revenue pickup. If the AED 134.3 Bn UAE backlog continues to release at its current pace and Dubai's Q2 2026 new-sales momentum is confirmed at the Q2 results, Q3 2026 is set up as a stronger print than Q2 — the YoY comparison base from Q3 2025 (AED 13,273 Mn) is demanding but not out of reach. The primary risk for Q3 2026 is a condensed delivery schedule: if milestones slip from Q2 into Q3, Q3 could be artificially elevated, and if Q3 milestones then slip into Q4, the full-year story becomes back-end loaded in a way that increases execution risk on the one quarter (Q4) that already carries the most weight.

---

## 10. Pre-Mortem

If this beat-favoring setup fails, the most likely reason is that the June 2026 consensus cut anticipated a structural deceleration in the Dubai off-plan cycle that this analysis underweights: unit volumes sold in FY2025 already fell −27% year-on-year (13,905 units vs 19,058 in FY2024), and if Q2 2026 new sales confirm a sustained volume decline that the AED value numbers are masking via ASP inflation, the analyst who cut from AED 2.46 to AED 1.93 on June 11 may prove to have been early rather than wrong. The second most likely reason we missed it is that construction cost inflation — the single biggest forward-looking margin risk identified in 03_margin-drivers.md — shows up visibly in Q2 2026 delivered gross margins before it is visible in the disclosed backlog-margin figure, creating a downside surprise on the EBITDA line that the consensus did not fully embed.

## earnings / 06_earnings-quality.md

_Source: `earnings/06_earnings-quality.md`_

# Earnings Quality — EMAR (Emaar Properties PJSC, DFM:EMAAR)

**Reporting standard:** IFRS | **Currency:** AED millions | **Fiscal year:** 31 December
**Sources:** Capital IQ & Proprietary Data export (FY2021–FY2025 + LTM Mar-31-2026) [CIQ Annual/Quarterly]; FY2025 Investor Presentation / Preliminary Annual Report (Feb-12-2026) [Inv Dec]; FY2024 Annual Report IFRS (Mar-14-2025) [AR24].
**Upstream dependency:** `01_historical-financials.md` — present and used throughout.

---

## 1. EBITDA → CFO → FCF Bridge (FY2021–FY2025)

All figures AED millions. Capex split (maintenance vs growth) is not separately disclosed by Emaar. Total capex is used throughout. *Capex split not disclosed — total capex used. FCF may understate true recurring free cash flow if a material portion of capex is growth-oriented (likely given the hotel/mall expansion programme).*

**Lead figure: Normalised operating FCF (FCF net of unearned revenue inflows).** Reported FCF is materially inflated every year by advance customer payments received under off-plan property contracts. These are real cash inflows but represent future delivery obligations (recognised as revenue only as construction milestones are reached over a 5–6 year delivery cycle under IFRS 15). Removing them gives the underlying recurring cash generation. Both figures are shown below, labelled.

| Item | FY2021 | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Trend |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| EBITDA (CIQ) | 7,803 | 9,332 | 14,405 | 17,563 | 24,132 | Accelerating |
| + Change in Unearned Revenue (buyer advance pmts) | 2,103 | 4,138 | 3,294 | 8,442 | 8,229 | Accelerating |
| +/− Other working capital change (ex-unearned) | −4,385 | 3,339 | 3,648 | 11,399 | 2,080 | Volatile |
| − Tax Paid | 0 | 0 | 0 | −224 | −844 | Deteriorating (new tax) |
| − Interest Paid | −974 | −809 | −921 | −855 | −1,002 | Stable |
| +/− Other operating items (non-cash, equity income, etc.) | 6,014 | 2,942 | −595 | −11,844 | 863 | Volatile |
| **CFO (as reported)** | **10,561** | **18,942** | **19,831** | **24,481** | **33,458** | **Accelerating** |
| − Capex (total; split not disclosed) | −1,288 | −960 | −578 | −534 | −934 | Stable/Low |
| **FCF — reported (CFO − Capex)** | **9,273** | **17,982** | **19,253** | **23,947** | **32,524** | **Accelerating** |
| − Change in Unearned Revenue (remove one-off advance inflows) | −2,103 | −4,138 | −3,294 | −8,442 | −8,229 | — |
| **FCF — normalised operating (lead figure)** | **7,170** | **13,844** | **15,959** | **15,505** | **24,295** | **Stable → Re-accelerating** |
| **CFO / EBITDA %** | **135%** | **203%** | **138%** | **139%** | **139%** | **Stable (excl. FY2022 spike)** |

*[Source: CIQ Annual Cash Flow, Income Statement; FY2021–FY2025. All figures computed from raw CIQ data.]*

**Key observations on the bridge:**

1. **FY2022 CFO/EBITDA of 203%** is anomalous. A large positive swing in other working capital items (AED 3,339 Mn ex-unearned) combined with record unearned revenue inflow (AED 4,138 Mn) pushed CFO far above EBITDA. This is not a recurring pattern.

2. **FY2021 and FY2024 "Other WC change"** swings are wide. FY2021 saw a AED −4,385 Mn drain; FY2024 saw a AED +11,399 Mn inflow. These reflect lumpiness in contract asset recognition (IFRS 15 percentage-of-completion timing) and payables. The underlying pattern is structural, not a quality red flag — it reflects the property developer model.

3. **Normalised FCF was roughly flat FY2022–FY2024** (AED 13.8 Bn → AED 15.5 Bn) despite strong EBITDA growth, because buyer advance payments are partly netted out. FY2025 showed re-acceleration to AED 24.3 Bn as EBITDA growth at scale outpaced the advance-payment component.

4. **Tax paid entered the bridge in FY2024 (AED 224 Mn) and rose sharply in FY2025 (AED 844 Mn)**. The effective tax rate moved from 1.5% (FY2023) → 7.7% (FY2024) → 13.0% (FY2025). This is a permanent structural change that will grow the CFO-to-EBITDA gap going forward.

---

## 2. Cash Conversion Assessment

CFO/EBITDA has held at 135%–139% in four of the five years shown (203% in FY2022 is the outlier). At first glance, CFO significantly above EBITDA appears extraordinary, but the mechanism is clear and disclosed: advance cash payments from off-plan property buyers inflate CFO before revenue is earned. This is not an earnings-quality concern; it is the natural consequence of Emaar's off-plan pre-sale model under IFRS 15.

On a normalised basis (removing unearned revenue inflows), CFO/EBITDA drops to approximately 97%–104% — a range consistent with a well-run developer with modest capex needs and low working capital intensity outside of the advance-payment cycle. This is healthy. There is no pattern of reported EBITDA failing to convert to cash; if anything, cash lands before earnings are recognised.

The trajectory of normalised FCF (AED 7.2 Bn → AED 24.3 Bn over five years) is broadly tracking EBITDA growth with a lag, consistent with the delivery cycle on the revenue backlog. No concern here.

---

## 3. Working Capital Trends

**Important context for DSO:** Emaar's accounts receivable under IFRS 15 consist primarily of contract assets (unbilled revenue recognised as construction milestones are completed, but not yet invoiced to buyers). These are structural and are settled over a 5–6 year delivery cycle — not traditional trade receivables collected in 30–90 days. DSO in absolute terms is very high (400–700 days) but this is the normal arithmetic for a property developer with a multi-year backlog, and the direction is the right one: DSO is falling as revenue accelerates faster than the AR balance.

| Metric | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | Direction | Risk |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Receivable days (DSO — short-term AR only) | 675 | 576 | 427 | Improving | Low (structural model; AR growing slower than revenue) |
| Inventory days (DIO) | 2 | 1 | 1 | Stable/declining | Low (negligible inventory for a developer) |
| Payable days (DPO) | 71 | 35 | 29 | Declining | Low-medium (payables being settled faster; no supplier-finance concern apparent) |
| Cash conversion cycle (DSO + DIO − DPO) | 607 | 542 | 399 | Improving | Low (improving trend driven by revenue outgrowing AR) |

*[Source: CIQ Annual Balance Sheet and Income Statement, FY2023–FY2025. DSO = short-term accounts receivable / (revenue ÷ 365). DIO = inventory / (COGS ÷ 365). DPO = accounts payable / (COGS ÷ 365).]*

**Flag assessments:**
- **DSO rising >10% YoY:** Not triggered. DSO is declining sharply (FY2023: 675 → FY2025: 427 days, −37%). Revenue is growing faster than the AR balance. AR grew +3.4% in FY2025 while revenue grew +39.6%. This is the opposite of a revenue-recognition concern.
- **DIO rising >15% YoY:** Not triggered. Inventory is negligible and declining.
- **DPO rising sharply:** Not triggered. DPO is declining (payables are being paid faster), which is a mild liquidity signal but not distress.

**Assessment of adjustments:** The single material adjustment (Company EBITDA vs CIQ EBITDA) is mechanically sound under IFRS and clearly disclosed. It adjusts for a non-cash item created by IFRS 9 discounting of long-term receivables. The adjustment is in the company's favour (higher EBITDA), it recurs every period, and at 5.9%–9.8% of reported EBITDA it is not immaterial. Users should be aware which figure they are quoting, but this is an accounting presentation difference, not an earnings manipulation.

---

## 9. Earnings Quality Score

**Score: 72 / 100**

*Band: 61–80 — Mostly clean, but some working capital or adjustment noise.*

**Primary reason for this score:** Emaar's GAAP earnings are substantially backed by real cash flows that arrive before income is recognised (the off-plan advance-payment model). The single biggest mechanical feature — CFO consistently far above EBITDA — is explained by structural buyer deposits, not by accounting manipulation. Receivables are improving relative to revenue. The EBITDA adjustment between CIQ and company figures is modest, mechanically sound, and disclosed. Deductions from a higher score: (1) the FY2021–FY2023 recurring "one-off" writedowns totalling AED 3.6 Bn, (2) growing non-operating income (interest on escrow + affiliate income) now contributing ~14% of reported net income and giving a structural flattery to EPS growth, (3) deferred contract costs growing faster than revenue, and (4) the new tax regime permanently reduces after-tax free cash flow and EPS growth relative to EBIT growth going forward — analysts using pre-FY2024 normalised multiples will overstate the quality-adjusted earnings.

---

## 10. The Single Biggest Quality Concern

The single most important risk that reported earnings overstate economic reality is the **inflation of reported CFO and headline FCF by off-plan buyer advance payments**. In FY2025, reported FCF was AED 32,524 Mn but normalised operating FCF — the cash the business generates before receiving buyer deposits for future-delivery projects — was AED 24,295 Mn, a gap of AED 8,229 Mn. Over FY2021–FY2025, cumulative advance payments from buyers that inflated reported FCF totalled AED 26,206 Mn. This cash is real but is not free: it is legally ring-fenced in project escrow accounts (AED 42,879 Mn restricted cash at FY2025 year-end) and must be used for construction. An analyst who values Emaar on a headline FCF yield basis without removing unearned-revenue inflows will significantly overstate the true recurring cash generation of the business. Similarly, the AED 2,505 Mn of interest income in FY2025 — earned on the large escrow and deposit balances — is non-recurring in the sense that it will shrink as projects are delivered and escrow balances are drawn down. These two items together (advance payments + escrow interest) mean that reported earnings at peak delivery and peak escrow will look artificially elevated versus the economic steady-state once the current backlog is delivered.

That said, this is a disclosure and model-understanding risk, not a fraud or manipulation risk. Emaar discloses the unearned revenue balance, the restricted cash balance, and the adjustment between reported and normalised EBITDA clearly in its investor presentations. The earnings are real and the cash conversion is genuine — the quality concern is one of investor interpretation, not accounting dishonesty.

---

*All figures computed from Capital IQ & Proprietary Data annual and quarterly exports (FY2021–FY2025). Numbers verified by reconciliation (computed CFO = reported CFO across all five years, zero residual). FY2024 audited IFRS annual report (Mar-14-2025) is available in the data pool in Arabic only; English-language accounting policy notes are not accessible, which is noted in the accrual quality section.*

## 1. Variable Selection

The 3–7 variables were drawn directly from the driver tables in `02_revenue-drivers.md` and `03_margin-drivers.md`, using magnitude ratings to rank order. The highest-magnitude variables from those tables are: (1) UAE Development backlog / POC delivery pace (magnitude: High, from both revenue and margin driver tables); (2) new property sales / buyer demand (magnitude: High, revenue table); (3) construction cost inflation on backlog (magnitude: High, margin table); (4) the UAE tax regime — Corporate Tax (9%) and DMTT (15%) (magnitude: High, margin table); (5) IFRS 15 POC project-mix timing and seasonality (magnitude: High for quarterly volatility, margin and revenue tables); (6) the EGP/AED foreign exchange rate on Emaar Misr (magnitude: Mid, both tables); and (7) Emaar Malls rent per sq. ft. / occupancy (magnitude: Mid, revenue and margin tables). The `10_external-dependency.md` output flagged the Dubai property demand cycle as the single biggest external lever and endorsed construction cost and FX as secondary exposures — consistent with the variable selection here. No variables have been invented outside the upstream driver tables.

The full FY2025 audited Annual Report was not in the data pool at the date of this analysis; accordingly, the IFRS 7 market-risk sensitivity tables (which would contain company-disclosed FX and interest-rate quantitative sensitivities) are unavailable. Where company-disclosed sensitivity exists in the preliminary results filing or investor presentation, it is used and labelled High confidence. Otherwise, the historical observed range or filing-supported inference is used, labelled Medium or Low.

---

## 4. The Single Highest-Sensitivity Variable

**The pace at which Emaar converts its AED 134.3 Bn UAE revenue backlog into recognised IFRS 15 revenue — through construction milestone certification — is the single variable that moves earnings the most.**

The current direction is positive: units delivered rose from 4,242 in FY2024 to 6,129 in FY2025 (+44%), and the Q4 POC pattern is accelerating as the 2021–2024 vintage of off-plan sales reaches construction completion. This variable is partly company-controlled (management sequences project launches and delivery timelines) and partly external (contractor capacity, building-material availability, government permitting speed). A ±15% shift in the annual rate of POC milestone certification moves EBITDA by approximately AED 2,500 Mn — equivalent to roughly 10% of FY2025 EBITDA — without any change in new sales. For the bear case to arrive: sustained construction slowdowns across the 50,800+ units under active development in the UAE (caused by contractor labour shortages, material cost disputes halting progress, or planning delays on large master-plan projects) would delay the quarterly certification of milestones. Because Q4 alone captures 32–33% of annual revenue through this mechanism, a disruption concentrated in Q4 milestone timing would have an outsized annual earnings effect — a Q4 delivery delay could shift AED 1–2 Bn of EBITDA from one year to the next with no change in underlying business value.

---

## 5. Interaction Effects

Two interaction effects are material and should be read together rather than independently.

First, the **backlog delivery pace and construction cost inflation compound each other**. A construction slowdown (the bear case for Variable 1) often arises from the same root cause as cost inflation (the bear case for Variable 6): contractor capacity tightness in a building boom. If Dubai's concurrent mega-projects (the AED 180 Bn Dubai Creek Harbour, the Al Maktoum Airport expansion, competitors' projects) strain labour supply, Emaar faces both slower delivery milestones AND higher contractor re-pricing simultaneously. In this compound scenario, EBITDA impact is not the sum of the two individual sensitivities (AED 2,500 + AED 175 Mn annually) applied independently — the delivery delay pushes the cost inflation into a compressed window, making the margin impact larger when units finally complete.

Second, **the Dubai property demand cycle (new sales) and POC delivery pace interact over a 3–4 year lag**. A demand decline in new sales today does not immediately cut EBITDA (the backlog absorbs it), but it reduces the future backlog accretion, meaning delivery pace will eventually slow as there are fewer units to build and deliver. The interaction creates a J-curve effect: near-term earnings stay high (backlog delivering), new sales slow (demand cycle peaks), then revenue falls 3–4 years later as the backlog depletes. This is not captured in the single-variable sensitivity table but is the key structural risk in the earnings outlook.

---

## 6. Non-Linear Or Asymmetric Risks

Three asymmetries are present in Emaar's sensitivity profile:

**1. Q4 concentration and delivery delay asymmetry (Variable 5 — POC timing):** Because Q4 captures 32–33% of annual revenue and EBITDA through IFRS 15 POC milestone timing, a delivery delay that pushes milestones into January (Q1 of the following year) creates a disproportionately large annual earnings miss. The upside is bounded (Q4 cannot easily exceed 35% share in a single year without a project-specific windfall), but the downside from a late Q4 delay is structurally larger. This is an asymmetric risk: a delay of a few weeks in construction certification can shift 2–3% of annual EBITDA from one year to the next.

**2. New sales to backlog to revenue: non-linear and lagged (Variable 2):** The backlog buffer creates a long, non-linear pathway from demand to earnings. A 30% decline in new sales does not produce a 30% EBITDA decline — it produces near-zero impact for 3 years, then a step-change decline as backlog depletes. The asymmetry is that investors may mis-price the lag: visible new-sales weakness years before the earnings impact arrives can depress the stock disproportionately (or be ignored too long if optimism prevails).

**3. EGP/AED FX: downside asymmetric (Variable 6):** The EGP has depreciated continuously against the AED since 2016. There is no structural reason for a sustained EGP strengthening; upside from EGP appreciation is historically rarer and shorter-lived than the downside from EGP depreciation. Emaar Misr's AED-reported EBITDA already collapsed from AED 1,559 Mn (96% margin, FY2024 — partly inflated by AED 650 Mn FX gain) to AED 479 Mn (31% margin, FY2025). If EGP depreciates a further 20–30%, the AED-translated EBITDA from Emaar Misr approaches zero or negative territory, removing a segment entirely from the earnings picture. The downside from further EGP weakness is therefore non-linear (can completely eliminate a segment's contribution) while the upside from EGP stability or modest strengthening is limited (already at suppressed margins).

---

## 7. Earnings Volatility Score

**Score: 38 / 100 (higher = WORSE — more volatile)**

**Band: Moderately stable — one or two variables matter but are manageable (21–40)**

**Reason:** Emaar's earnings are substantially insulated from short-term external volatility by two structural features — the AED 134.3 Bn revenue backlog (which locks in 3–4 years of revenue regardless of new sales), and the recurring-business EBITDA floor (Emaar Malls at 86% EBITDA margin contributing AED 4,935 Mn, Hospitality at 48% contributing AED 1,109 Mn). These together provide a durable base. The key swing variable — POC delivery pace — is partly company-controlled and historically stable within a 10–15% band in any given year outside of a COVID-scale external event. The main sources of volatility that push the score above 20 are: (i) Q4 POC concentration creates quarter-to-quarter swings that can look like earnings misses but are timing effects; (ii) the tax regime step-change (DMTT) is now embedded and will not create additional noise unless further expanded; and (iii) EGP/AED FX is an ongoing source of headline noise at the sub-segment level. The score is held at 38 rather than a higher number because the AED 134.3 Bn backlog is the clearest earnings-smoothing mechanism in the data pool — it would require a multi-year disruption (not a single-quarter event) to materially erode the earnings trajectory.
